Many functions that keep an organism alive—such as obtaining and using energy or removing waste—happen inside its cells. Though these processes may also occur within larger organ systems, the cell is the smallest unit that can carry them out.

contents.text: Both prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells are surrounded by a cell membrane, are filled with cytoplasm, and contain ribosomes. But only eukaryotic cells contain linear chromosomes stored inside a membrane-bound nucleus; DNA in prokaryotic cells forms a continuous loop and is located in a central area that is not surrounded by a nuclear membrane.
Prokaryotic cells comprise, or make up, only unicellular organisms, while eukaryotic cells comprise both unicellular and multicellular organisms.

Unicellular organisms can be prokaryotic or eukaryotic, but all complex multicellular organisms are made up of eukaryotic cells. In general, prokaryotic cells are smaller and structurally less complex than eukaryotic cells, but they have more diverse ways to get energy and process nutrients. For example, there are prokaryotic organisms that can make their own food from carbon dioxide gas and therefore can live in extreme places that are inhospitable to most other organisms.

have any membrane-bound organelles or a nucleus.

contents.text: Eukaryotic cells do have membrane-bound organelles and a nucleus that contains linear chromosomes. Some eukaryotic cells, such as plant cells, have a cell wall.
